chapter.name: Electromagnetic Waves
chapter.blurb: The chapter shows how Maxwell removed an inconsistency in Ampere's circuital law by introducing the displacement current, giving the Ampere-Maxwell law and a symmetry between changing electric and magnetic fields. It then describes, mostly qualitatively, how accelerated charges radiate electromagnetic waves, in which E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel and which move in vacuum at c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) with B0 = E0/c. Finally it surveys the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays, with how each region is produced, detected and used.

scope_in.item: Explain the inconsistency in Ampere's circuital law for a charging capacitor using surfaces with the same rim, and how the missing term is found from the electric flux Q/epsilon0 between the plates

State and use the displacement current i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt (including epsilon0 A dE/dt and C dV/dt for a capacitor) and recognise that it is due to a time-varying electric field and is a source of magnetic field like a conduction current
State and apply the Ampere-Maxwell law with total current i_c + i_d; say where conduction and displacement currents exist for a charging capacitor; find B outside and between circular plates

Explain the symmetry between Faraday's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law (time-dependent E and B give rise to each other), why it is not perfect (no magnetic monopoles), and recognise the four Maxwell's equations in vacuum by name

Explain that only accelerated (for example oscillating) charges radiate electromagnetic waves, that the wave has the frequency of the oscillating charge and takes its energy from the source, and why the demonstration came in the radio region (Hertz), with the contributions of Bose and Marconi

Describe the nature of electromagnetic waves: E and B perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (E x B along propagation), no material medium, carry energy; use c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) and v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) in a medium
Use Ex = E0 sin(kz - omega t), By = B0 sin(kz - omega t), k = 2 pi/lambda, omega = ck, nu lambda = c and B0 = E0/c to find wavelength, frequency, amplitudes and field expressions

Name the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order, and give for each its production, detection and uses as stated in Sections 8.4.1-8.4.7 and Table 8.1; place a wavelength that lies clearly inside a region

concepts.name: Displacement current
concepts.description: The inconsistency in Ampere's circuital law for a charging capacitor and the displacement current, epsilon0 times the rate of change of electric flux, that removes it.
concepts.idea: A time-varying electric field behaves like a current: between the plates of a charging capacitor no charge flows, yet the changing electric flux there counts as a displacement current equal to the charging current.
concepts.rule: Ampere's circuital law applied to a loop around the wire of a charging capacitor gives B(2 pi r) = mu0 i for a flat surface cut by the wire, but zero for a pot-shaped or tiffin-box-shaped surface with the same rim that passes between the plates, because no conduction current crosses it. The field at a point cannot depend on the surface chosen, so the law is missing a term. Between the plates E = Q/(A epsilon0), so the electric flux is Phi_E = Q/epsilon0 and epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt = dQ/dt = i. The displacement current is i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt, measured in ampere. It is due to a time-varying electric field, not to moving charges, and it acts as a source of magnetic field in exactly the same way as a conduction current. It is zero wherever the electric field does not change with time. For a capacitor, i_d = epsilon0 A dE/dt = C dV/dt.
concepts.example: A 100 pF capacitor whose voltage rises at 2.0 x 10^5 V/s carries a displacement current C dV/dt = 2.0 x 10^-5 A between its plates.

At a certain instant the plates of a parallel plate capacitor carry a charge of magnitude 8.85 x 10^-9 C. Take epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2. Find the electric flux through a flat surface lying between the plates and covering the whole plate area.
questions.a: Between the plates E = Q/(A epsilon0), uniform over the plate area A, so Phi_E = E A = Q/epsilon0. Phi_E = (8.85 x 10^-9 C)/(8.85 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2) = 1.0 x 10^3 N m^2/C (that is, 1000 V m).
s: Phi_E = E A = Q/epsilon0

questions.q: A displacement current of 1.0 A is to be set up between the plates of a capacitor of capacitance 1 microfarad. At what rate must the potential difference across the capacitor change?

A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.01 m^2 separated by 1.0 mm of air. The potential difference between the plates is increased at a steady rate of 2.0 x 10^6 V/s. Take epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2. Find (a) the rate of change of the electric field between the plates and (b) the displacement current between the plates.
questions.a: (a) E = V/d, so dE/dt = (dV/dt)/d = (2.0 x 10^6 V/s)/(1.0 x 10^-3 m) = 2.0 x 10^9 V/m s. (b) Phi_E = E A, so i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt = epsilon0 A dE/dt = 8.85 x 10^-12 x 0.01 x 2.0 x 10^9 = 1.77 x 10^-4 A.
s: dE/dt = (dV/dt)/d = 2.0 x 10^9 V/m s, with d converted to 1.0 x 10^-3 m
i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt = epsilon0 A dE/dt

questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor is being charged by a current i = dQ/dt. Starting from the electric flux between the plates, show that the displacement current between the plates is equal to i.
questions.a: The flux between the plates is Phi_E = E A = [Q/(A epsilon0)] A = Q/epsilon0. Differentiating, dPhi_E/dt = (1/epsilon0) dQ/dt. Hence i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt = dQ/dt = i.
s: Phi_E = Q/epsilon0 between the plates
i_d = epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt = dQ/dt = i

questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance 100 pF is connected to a source whose voltage rises at a steady rate from 0 to 300 V in 1.0 ms and then stays constant at 300 V. Analyse the displacement current between the plates during the rise and after it.
questions.a: During the rise dV/dt = 300 V/(1.0 x 10^-3 s) = 3.0 x 10^5 V/s. Since Q = CV, i_d = dQ/dt = C dV/dt = 100 x 10^-12 F x 3.0 x 10^5 V/s = 3.0 x 10^-5 A (30 microampere), constant throughout the rise. After the voltage becomes constant the electric field between the plates no longer changes, so the electric flux is constant and the displacement current is zero.
s: dV/dt = 3.0 x 10^5 V/s during the rise
i_d = C dV/dt = 3.0 x 10^-5 A during the rise
After the rise the field is steady, so i_d = 0

questions.q: A student argues: 'Nothing flows between the plates of a capacitor, so it is wrong to call the term Maxwell added a current.' Evaluate this argument.
questions.a: The student is right that no charge flows between the plates, but the name is justified. The term, epsilon0 times the rate of change of electric flux, has the dimensions of a current, equals the charging current i in the wire, and produces a magnetic field in exactly the same way as a conduction current. It is called a displacement current to distinguish it from a conduction current due to flow of charges.
s: Concedes that no charge flows - it is not a conduction current
Justifies the name: it equals i and is a source of magnetic field exactly as a conduction current is

questions.q: Design an experimental check, using a parallel plate capacitor that is being charged, which would show that the displacement current is real. State what you would measure, where, and what result would support Maxwell's idea.
questions.a: Charge a parallel plate capacitor with a time-varying current. Measure the magnetic field at a point M between the plates and at a point P just outside the plates, both at the same distance from the axis of the wire. No conduction current flows between the plates, so the original Ampere's law would predict no magnetic field at M. If the field measured at M is found to be the same as that at P, the changing electric field between the plates must be acting as a current, which confirms the displacement current.
s: Set-up: capacitor being charged, magnetic field measured at a point between the plates
Comparison point just outside the plates at the same distance from the axis
Expected result: the two fields are the same, though no conduction current crosses the gap

concepts.name: The Ampere-Maxwell law and Maxwell's equations
concepts.description: Total current as the sum of conduction and displacement currents, the generalised Ampere's circuital law, its symmetry with Faraday's law and the four Maxwell's equations in vacuum.
concepts.idea: The source of a magnetic field is the total current, conduction plus displacement, so a changing electric field produces a magnetic field just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.
concepts.rule: Total current i = i_c + i_d = i_c + epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt. Outside the plates of a charging capacitor i_c = i and i_d = 0; between the plates i_c = 0 and i_d = i. The Ampere-Maxwell law: closed line integral of B.dl = mu0 i_c + mu0 epsilon0 dPhi_E/dt, where the total current is that through any surface having the loop as its perimeter, so every such surface gives the same result. The field at a point just inside the plates is the same as that just outside. For circular plates of radius R with uniform field, a loop of radius r < R between the plates encloses displacement current i r^2/R^2, so B = mu0 i r/(2 pi R^2); outside, B = mu0 i/(2 pi r). Both currents may be present in the same region since no medium is a perfect conductor or perfect insulator; in regions with only time-varying electric fields there is only displacement current, and still a magnetic field. Faraday's law says a changing magnetic field gives an electric field; the symmetrical counterpart is that a changing electric field gives a magnetic field. The symmetry is not perfect: there are no known magnetic monopoles. Maxwell's equations in vacuum: Gauss's law for electricity, Gauss's law for magnetism, Faraday's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law.
concepts.example: Circular capacitor plates of radius 6 cm are charged by a current of 1.2 A. A loop of radius 3 cm between the plates encloses a displacement current 1.2 x (3/6)^2 = 0.3 A, so B = (2 x 10^-7 x 0.3)/0.03 = 2 x 10^-6 T there (using mu0/(2 pi) = 2 x 10^-7 T m/A).

questions.a: The displacement current is spread uniformly over the plate area, so the loop encloses the fraction (area of loop)/(area of plate) = (R/2)^2/R^2 = 1/4 of it. Enclosed displacement current = 0.8 A x 1/4 = 0.2 A.

A loop of radius r = 0.05 m encloses i_d = 2 A x (0.05/0.10)^2 = 0.5 A. By symmetry B is the same all round the loop, so B(2 pi r) = mu0 x 0.5 A. B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 0.5)/(2 pi x 0.05) = 2 x 10^-6 T.

By the Ampere-Maxwell law the displacement current is a source of magnetic field just as a conduction current is, so a magnetic field exists.
s: A time-varying electric field gives a displacement current although the conduction current is zero

questions.q: A capacitor with circular plates of radius R = 4 cm is being charged by a current of 0.6 A, the electric field being uniform between the plates and zero outside the plate area. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Compare the magnetic field, in the plane midway between the plates, at distances 2 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm from the axis.
questions.a: At r = 4 cm (= R) the loop encloses all the displacement current: B = mu0 i/(2 pi R) = (2 x 10^-7 x 0.6)/0.04 = 3.0 x 10^-6 T. At r = 2 cm the loop encloses 0.6 x (2/4)^2 = 0.15 A: B = (2 x 10^-7 x 0.15)/0.02 = 1.5 x 10^-6 T. At r = 8 cm the loop still encloses only 0.6 A: B = (2 x 10^-7 x 0.6)/0.08 = 1.5 x 10^-6 T. The field rises in proportion to r up to the edge of the plates, is largest there, and falls as 1/r beyond; the values at 2 cm and 8 cm are equal, each half the value at the edge.
s: B at 4 cm = 3.0 x 10^-6 T (all 0.6 A enclosed)
B at 2 cm = 1.5 x 10^-6 T (0.15 A enclosed)
B at 8 cm = 1.5 x 10^-6 T; largest at the edge, equal at 2 cm and 8 cm

questions.q: A student says: 'Maxwell showed that Ampere's circuital law was wrong, so every result obtained from it for steady currents must be discarded.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is not justified. For steady currents the electric field does not change with time, so the displacement current is zero and the Ampere-Maxwell law reduces exactly to the original Ampere's circuital law. The original law was incomplete only for time-varying electric fields; its results for steady currents remain valid.
s: For steady currents the displacement current is zero, so the generalised law reduces to the original one
Judgement: the law was incomplete, not wrong for steady currents; those results stand

questions.q: Write a short explanatory note that links Faraday's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law to show how time-dependent electric and magnetic fields give rise to each other, and state the important consequence of this symmetry.
questions.a: Faraday's law: an emf is induced equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux; since an emf implies an electric field, a magnetic field changing with time gives rise to an electric field. Ampere-Maxwell law: because the displacement current is a source of magnetic field, an electric field changing with time gives rise to a magnetic field. So time-dependent electric and magnetic fields give rise to each other. The important consequence is the existence of electromagnetic waves, coupled time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate in space.
s: Faraday's law: a changing magnetic field gives rise to an electric field
Ampere-Maxwell law: a changing electric field (displacement current) gives rise to a magnetic field
Consequence: the fields sustain each other, so electromagnetic waves exist

concepts.name: Sources of electromagnetic waves
concepts.description: Accelerated charges as the source of electromagnetic waves, the frequency and energy of the radiated wave, and the experiments of Hertz, Bose and Marconi.
concepts.idea: Only accelerated charges radiate: an oscillating charge sets up oscillating electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other and travel away as a wave of the same frequency.
concepts.rule: Stationary charges produce only electrostatic fields and charges in uniform motion (steady currents) produce magnetic fields that do not vary with time, so neither is a source of electromagnetic waves. Accelerated charges radiate electromagnetic waves; an oscillating charge is an accelerating charge. The oscillating electric field produces an oscillating magnetic field, which in turn produces an oscillating electric field, and so on. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge, and the energy of the wave comes at the expense of the energy of the source. An electric dipole is a basic source of electromagnetic waves. Light cannot be produced by an ac circuit: yellow light has a frequency of about 6 x 10^14 Hz, while even modern electronic circuits reach hardly about 10^11 Hz, so the demonstration came in the radio wave region, in Hertz's experiment (waves of the order of a few metres). Jagdish Chandra Bose produced and observed much shorter waves (25 mm to 5 mm) in the laboratory; Marconi transmitted waves over many kilometres, the beginning of communication using electromagnetic waves.
concepts.example: A charge oscillating at 10^9 Hz radiates an electromagnetic wave of the same frequency, 10^9 Hz.

questions.q: A charge is made to oscillate about a fixed point at 2 x 10^9 Hz. Explain step by step how this produces an electromagnetic wave, state the frequency of the wave, and state where the energy of the wave comes from.
questions.a: An oscillating charge is an accelerating charge, so it radiates. It produces an oscillating electric field in space; this produces an oscillating magnetic field, which in turn is a source of an oscillating electric field, and so on, so the two fields regenerate each other as the wave propagates. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge, 2 x 10^9 Hz. The energy carried by the wave comes at the expense of the energy of the source, the accelerated charge.
s: Oscillating (accelerated) charge gives oscillating E, which gives oscillating B, which gives E again - the fields regenerate each other
Frequency of the wave = 2 x 10^9 Hz
Energy comes from the source, the accelerated charge

An accelerated charge produces time-varying electric and magnetic fields and so radiates electromagnetic waves.
s: Stationary charge: electrostatic field only; steady current: magnetic field that does not vary with time

questions.q: It might seem that the prediction that light is an electromagnetic wave could be tested simply by setting up an ac circuit that oscillates at the frequency of yellow light, about 6 x 10^14 Hz. questions.a: An ac circuit radiates waves at the frequency at which its current oscillates. Even modern electronic circuits give frequencies of hardly about 10^11 Hz, thousands of times lower than the 6 x 10^14 Hz of yellow light, so a circuit cannot be made to oscillate at optical frequencies. The test therefore had to come in the low-frequency radio wave region: Hertz produced and detected electromagnetic waves in the laboratory, verifying the basic prediction of Maxwell's equations.

Circuits reach only about 10^11 Hz, far below 6 x 10^14 Hz

Accelerated (oscillating) charges radiate, and the frequency of the wave equals the frequency of oscillation of the charges, so the wave has frequency 100 MHz. A battery gives a steady current: charges in uniform motion produce a magnetic field that does not vary with time, so no electromagnetic wave is radiated.

Oscillation frequency must be 100 MHz because wave frequency = charge frequency
Steady current gives a magnetic field that does not vary with time - no radiation

concepts.name: Nature and speed of electromagnetic waves
concepts.description: The transverse nature of electromagnetic waves, the directions of E, B and propagation, and the speed of the waves in vacuum and in a material medium.
concepts.idea: In an electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, need no material medium, and move in vacuum at c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0).
concepts.rule: E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation; the direction of E x B is the direction of propagation. For a plane wave along z with E along x, B is along y, and both vary as sin(kz - omega t), so they reach their maxima and zeros together. Electromagnetic waves are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space; no material medium is involved. Speed in vacuum c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0), about 3 x 10^8 m/s, equal to the speed of light from optical measurements and the same for all wavelengths; its constancy is used to define a standard of length. In a material medium of permittivity epsilon and permeability mu, v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon), so the speed depends on the electric and magnetic properties of the medium. Electromagnetic waves carry energy from one place to another.
concepts.example: In a medium with permittivity 25 epsilon0 and permeability mu0 the speed of an electromagnetic wave is c/sqrt(25) = (3 x 10^8)/5 = 0.6 x 10^8 m/s.

questions.q: Medium P has permittivity 16 epsilon0 and permeability mu0. Medium Q has permittivity 4 epsilon0 and permeability 4 mu0. Take c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Find the speed of electromagnetic waves in each medium and comment on the result.

The speeds are equal although the media are different, because the speed depends only on the product of the permeability and the permittivity, which is 16 mu0 epsilon0 in both.

Each field varies sinusoidally with z at a given time
Same sine factor: maxima and zeros of E and B occur at the same places

concepts.name: Equations and wave relations of a plane electromagnetic wave
concepts.description: The sinusoidal expressions for E and B in a plane electromagnetic wave and the relations between wave number, angular frequency, frequency, wavelength and the two amplitudes.
concepts.idea: A plane electromagnetic wave is described by E0 sin(kz - omega t) and B0 sin(kz - omega t); its frequency and wavelength are tied together by c, and its two amplitudes by B0 = E0/c.
concepts.rule: Ex = E0 sin(kz - omega t), By = B0 sin(kz - omega t). k = 2 pi/lambda is the magnitude of the wave vector, whose direction is the direction of propagation; omega = 2 pi nu is the angular frequency; the speed of propagation is omega/k. In vacuum omega = ck, that is nu x lambda = c, and B0 = E0/c. A phase (kx - omega t) describes a wave travelling along +x and (kx + omega t) one travelling along -x. The same expression can be written as sin[2 pi (z/lambda - t/T)] with T = 1/nu.
concepts.example: A wave of frequency 25 MHz in vacuum has wavelength c/nu = (3 x 10^8)/(25 x 10^6) = 12 m; if its electric field amplitude is 6.3 V/m, its magnetic field amplitude is E0/c = 6.3/(3 x 10^8) = 2.1 x 10^-8 T.

concepts.name: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.description: The regions of the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays: their order, how each is produced and detected, and their uses, as stated in the chapter and its Table 8.1.
concepts.idea: All electromagnetic waves are the same kind of wave travelling at the same speed in vacuum; they are given different names according to wavelength, roughly by how they are produced and detected.
concepts.rule: In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. There is no sharp division between regions, and they overlap. Table 8.1: radio (> 0.1 m) - rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in aerials, detected by receiver's aerials; microwave (0.1 m to 1 mm) - klystron or magnetron valve, point contact diodes; infrared (1 mm to 700 nm) - vibration of atoms and molecules, thermopiles, bolometer, infrared photographic film; light (700 nm to 400 nm) - electrons in atoms moving to a lower energy level, the eye, photocells, photographic film; ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm) - inner shell electrons moving to a lower level, photocells, photographic film; X-rays (1 nm to 10^-3 nm) - X-ray tubes or inner shell electrons, photographic film, Geiger tubes, ionisation chamber; gamma rays (< 10^-3 nm) - radioactive decay of the nucleus. Uses: radio and TV communication, cellular phones (radio); radar, speed guns, microwave ovens tuned to the resonant frequency of water molecules (microwaves); physical therapy, remote controls, satellite detectors, the greenhouse effect (infrared, the 'heat waves'); LASIK eye surgery, killing germs in water purifiers (ultraviolet, absorbed by the ozone layer and by ordinary glass); medical diagnosis and treatment of some cancers (X-rays); destroying cancer cells (gamma rays).
concepts.example: A wave of frequency 5 x 10^12 Hz has wavelength (3 x 10^8)/(5 x 10^12) = 6 x 10^-5 m = 60 micrometre, which lies in the infrared region.

questions.q: (I) X-rays are used only as a diagnostic tool and never for treatment. (II) The infrared band lies adjacent to the low-frequency (long-wavelength) end of the visible spectrum. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Using Table 8.1 of the chapter on electromagnetic waves, compare radio waves and gamma rays in terms of how each is produced and how each is detected.
questions.a: Radio waves are produced by rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in aerials and are detected by receiver's aerials. Gamma rays are produced by radioactive decay of the nucleus and are detected by photographic film, Geiger tubes or an ionisation chamber. So radio waves come from charges moving in circuits, while gamma rays come from the nucleus.
s: Radio: electrons accelerated and decelerated in aerials; detected by receiver's aerials
Gamma: radioactive decay of the nucleus; detected by photographic film, Geiger tubes or ionisation chamber

questions.q: Three sources emit electromagnetic waves in vacuum with frequencies 1 x 10^6 Hz, 3 x 10^10 Hz and 6 x 10^14 Hz. Take c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Find the wavelength of each and, using the wavelength ranges of Table 8.1, assign each to its region of the spectrum.
questions.a: lambda = c/nu. For 1 x 10^6 Hz: lambda = 300 m, greater than 0.1 m, so radio. For 3 x 10^10 Hz: lambda = 0.01 m = 1 cm, between 0.1 m and 1 mm, so microwave. For 6 x 10^14 Hz: lambda = 5 x 10^-7 m = 500 nm, between 700 nm and 400 nm, so visible light.
s: 300 m - radio
0.01 m (1 cm) - microwave
5 x 10^-7 m (500 nm) - visible light

questions.q: A student notices that the text and Table 8.1 of the chapter on electromagnetic waves give different limits for where the ultraviolet region ends and the X-ray region begins, and concludes that one of them must be a misprint. Evaluate this conclusion.
questions.a: The conclusion is not justified. The chapter states that there is no sharp division between one kind of wave and the next and that the regions overlap. The names are assigned roughly according to how the waves are produced and/or detected, so quoted limits are only approximate and can differ.
s: The regions have no sharp boundaries and overlap
Judgement: differing limits are not an error - classification is rough, by production and detection

questions.q: Prepare a summary chart, written as three lines, for microwaves, infrared waves and ultraviolet rays, giving for each one way it is produced and one use, as stated in the chapter on electromagnetic waves.
questions.a: Microwaves - produced by special vacuum tubes (klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes); used in radar systems for aircraft navigation (or microwave ovens, speed guns). Infrared - produced by hot bodies and molecules (vibration of atoms and molecules); used in physical therapy lamps (or remote switches, satellite detectors). Ultraviolet - produced by special lamps and very hot bodies such as the sun; used in LASIK eye surgery (or to kill germs in water purifiers).
s: Microwaves: klystron/magnetron source and a correct use (radar, oven, speed gun)
Infrared: hot bodies/vibrating molecules and a correct use (therapy, remotes, satellites)
Ultraviolet: special lamps/very hot bodies and a correct use (LASIK, water purifiers)
